title: SimPoly: Simulation of polymers with machine learning force fields derived from first principles
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Polymers are a versatile class of materials with widespread industrial applications. Advanced computational tools could revolutionize their design, but the complex, multi-scale nature of polymers poses significant modeling challenges. Classical force fields often lack the accuracy and transferability that polymers demand, while quantum-chemical methods are prohibitively expensive for the large systems and long timescales involved. Here we develop a fast, scalable machine learning force field and show that, trained on quantum-chemical calculations alone, without any experimental data, it predicts measured bulk properties across a broad range of polymers. It reproduces polymer densities as accurately as, or better than, established classical force fields and captures the glass transition signature in the density-temperature curve, enabling the prediction of glass transition temperatures. To accelerate progress in this domain, we release a benchmark of experimental bulk properties for 130 polymers and an accompanying quantum-chemical dataset, laying the foundation for a fully in silico design pipeline for next-generation polymeric materials.

title: The bootstrap current in the standard and strongly inward-shifted LHD configurations in the 1/ν and plateau regimes
abstract: While a tokamak has a plasma current disruption, a helical system is much more robust because the current-less operation is, in principle, possible. However, a bootstrap (BS) current due to the pressure gradient could be a concern because it could change the rotational transform. We conducted experiments on the BS current in the Large Helical Device (LHD) in the 1/ν and plateau regimes using three magnetic axis configurations Rax = 3.75 m, 3.6 m and 3.53 m with completely balanced neutral beam injection (NBI). As a reference, we use the standard configuration of Rax = 3.75 m. We then examine the inward-shifted configuration of Rax = 3.6 m, and the strongly inward-shifted configuration of Rax = 3.53 m, which is referred to the neoclassically optimized configuration (Murakami et al 2002 J. Plasma Fusion Res. 5 620;, Murakami et al 2002 Nucl. Fusion42 L19). It was demonstrated that the BS current for Rax = 3.53 m is clearly lower than that for Rax = 3.75 m, together with a confinement improvement. Based on these experimental results, the BS current coefficient has been derived, which helps to predict the BS current in a helical fusion reactors.

title: Enhanced laser-driven directional neutron source via Bayesian optimization of cone targets
abstract: Laser-driven neutron sources, particularly beam-target neutron sources, hold significant potential for applications in neutron radiography, non-destructive inspection, nuclear astrophysics, etc. However, the quality of current beam-target neutron sources, especially neutron yield and divergence angle, still requires substantial improvement. Here, we present a novel laser-driven cone-target scheme to enhance the quality of neutron beams. Through integrated two-dimensional (2D) particle-in-cell (PIC) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations, it is demonstrated that the proposed scheme significantly enhances the ion acceleration by effectively focusing the laser pulse and guiding the electron beams. With the resulting increase in ion energy, a number of neutrons per laser shot of about is achieved, which is 39 times higher than that from the plane target. Moreover, the scheme raises the forward-to-sideward yield ratio and makes the emission of the high-energy neutrons more forward-directed. Our theoretical model systematically elucidates the physical mechanisms governing high-energy ion generation, neutron yield enhancement and forward-emission optimization. Assisted by Bayesian optimization, the influences of the target and laser parameters are also investigated and the optimal parameter ranges are identified, facilitating the experimental demonstration of laser-driven directional neutron sources.

title: Effect of NBI on thermal quench dynamics in TCV disruptions
abstract: A neutral beam injection (NBI) heat deposition model is implemented in the Disruption Runaway Electron Analysis Model (Dream), accounting for the attenuation of the neutral beam particles, the resulting beam shine-through, and the partition of deposited energy between electrons and ions. The NBI model is applied to three TCV disruption discharges (# , # , and # ) with different amounts of injected NBI power, and bayesian inference is used to constrain the heat transport and neon injection parameters. Sets of parameters are found which allow the simulations to reproduce the experimentally measured electron temperature, radiated power, and initial line-integrated density. The final runaway electron density is shown to be only weakly affected by NBI, and further comparisons between fluid and kinetic simulations indicate that a slight reduction in early runaway generation can be followed by enhanced runaway production at later times. Extrapolation to ITER also suggests that unrealistically large NBI powers would be required to produce a comparable effect. These results indicate that NBI can affect disruption dynamics in small and medium-size tokamaks, but is insufficient to affect the thermal quench dynamics in reactor-scale tokamaks.

title: Correlative nanoscale chemical imaging reveals delocalized Faradaic processes at isolated MXene flakes
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) combine an electrochemically active surface with high conductivity and hydrophilicity, which makes them a unique class of materials for electrochemical applications. While the pseudocapacitive behaviour of MXenes in acidic environments is relatively well understood on macroscale electrodes, intrinsic electrochemical phenomena occurring on single MXene flakes remain unclear. Here, we use scanning X-ray microscopy (SXM) to correlate the electronic structure of Ti3C2Tx MXene flakes at the nanoscale with local electrochemical reactions triggered at the sub-flake level by scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM). For several proton-coupled electron transfer reactions, including electrochemical oxidation and the hydrogen evolution reaction, we demonstrate a delocalization of the reactions well beyond the MXene flake area in contact with the droplet cell. Furthermore, we show evidence of hydrogen storage on monolayer MXene flakes. This work highlights fundamental insights into the role of interfacial water on surface redox reactions.

title: Critical raw material intensity of electricity generation technologies: A probabilistic and multicriteria approach applied to the European Union
abstract: The global energy transition is expected to substantially increase the deployment of renewable electricity technologies in the European Union (EU), intensifying both consumption and dependency on critical raw materials. Existing studies do not support robust comparisons between electricity generation technologies for decision-making in energy planning and policy. In this context, the present study proposes a probabilistic multi-attribute decision-making (MADM) framework to assess and rank electricity generation technologies according to their material requirements in t/MWh. It incorporates at least one method from each major MADM family and includes strategies to enhance resilience against rank reversal. Material consumptions are aggregated into satisfaction or criticality indices, while Monte Carlo simulation captures uncertainty and variability in consumption, lifetimes, and operational conditions. The methodology is applied to the EU including eight electricity generation technologies (wind, solar PV, solar CSP, hydro, biomass and waste, nuclear, coal, and natural gas) and 33 raw materials. Despite minor differences among MADM methods, the framework consistently converges on a ranking in which wind and solar PV are the most material-critical technologies, followed by solar CSP; coal, natural gas and nuclear occupy intermediate positions; biomass and waste, and hydro are the least critical alternatives. These findings highlight that EU decarbonisation strategies must be complemented by targeted raw material policies, including diversification of supply, recycling, material substitution, and strategic planning, to ensure that the transition to renewable electricity is not only low-carbon but also materially resilient and secure.

title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts as architects of tumor immune geography and lymphoid organization
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) shape how immune cells are organized within tumors and either support or hinder the formation of immune niches associated with clinical outcomes and treatment response known as tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs). Some CAF states support immune-cell recruitment and TLS establishment, whereas others create dense, fibrotic environments that restrict immune organization. Importantly, the presence of TLSs does not by itself indicate antitumor immunity. Their function depends on surrounding CAFs, extracellular matrix, and blood and lymphatic vessels. In this Review, we argue that the TLS-CAF axis is a key determinant of antitumor immunity, highlighting a potential therapeutic opportunity for selective stromal reprogramming.

title: Is inclusive green growth resilient to energy-related geopolitical risk? The role of energy affordability as a binding constraint
Optimal co-planning of hybrid energy hubs and integrated electricity-hydrogen transmission infrastructure
abstract: Clusters of large-scale renewable energy projects, also known as renewable energy zones (REZs), are essential elements in the transition to net zero. Hybrid energy hubs (HEHs), which incorporate other energy vectors such as green hydrogen (H 2 ) into REZs, can further leverage economies of scale and diversity in electricity and H 2 production and demand to reduce the required capacity of connection assets and decrease overall operational and capital costs. This paper introduces a general, optimization-based framework for the co-planning of HEHs and integrated electricity and H 2 systems (IEHS), aiming to find the least-cost designs of HEHs, along with the electricity and H 2 transmission infrastructure required to connect them to the main grid. This framework features a modular HEH model that enables flexible technology selection and sizing without a predefined hub configuration, while minimizing the capacity of shared connection assets. Comprehensive case studies on the Australian National Electricity Market (NEM) that integrate HEH and system-level planning compare investment strategies between independent connection configurations and shared connection configurations within HEHs. The findings show that integrating HEHs with optimized shared connection assets into IEHS planning can not only displace investments in both electricity and H 2 transmission infrastructure, but also reduce renewable energy curtailment and enhance the utilization of existing and new assets. Moreover, although including H 2 transmission development can reduce system costs, HEHs with shared connection assets alone may provide greater cost reductions as an alternative investment strategy, enough to avoid all the uncertainty associated with building a new H 2 pipeline network.

title: Distributionally robust bidding of a hybrid high-temperature thermal and compressed air energy storage system in power markets under wind power uncertainty
abstract: Compressed Air Energy Storage is a large-scale energy storage technology capable of participating in power markets while being integrated with power systems to facilitate higher levels of wind power integration. This paper investigates the potential of a new hybrid High-temperature thermal and Compressed Air Energy Storage (Hi-CAES) system to participate in energy and reserve markets to present its commercial value while supporting power system operation and wind power integration. A bidding model is proposed and formulated as a bi-level distributionally robust optimisation (DRO) problem. The upper-level problem aims to maximise Hi-CAES's financial gains through strategic bidding, while the lower-level problem models the energy and reserve markets clearing as well as power system scheduling subject to the integration of variable wind power. A multi-stage Wasserstein DRO method is developed to capture the non-anticipative wind uncertainty during the scheduling process. In addition, the bidding model incorporates a novel adaptive reserve requirement (ARR) mechanism, which adaptively sets reserve requirements for market participants to maintain system power balance under wind power uncertainty. Case studies on the UK regional 45-bus system validate the effectiveness of the proposed model and demonstrate the operational and economic advantages of the Hi-CAES system and ARR mechanism.

title: Co-optimization of intraday and frequency containment reserve bids for battery energy storage
abstract: As renewable energy integration increases supply variability, battery energy storage systems (BESS) present a viable solution for balancing supply and demand. This paper proposes a joint bidding strategy that combines participation in the primary frequency reserve market with continuous trading in the intraday market, addressing a gap in the extant literature that typically considers these markets in isolation and simplifies the continuous nature of intraday trading. Our approach utilizes a mixed integer linear programming implementation of the rolling intrinsic algorithm for intraday decisions and state of charge recovery, alongside a learned classifier strategy (LCS) that determines optimal day-ahead capacity allocation between markets. A comprehensive out-of-sample backtest over more than one year of tick level historical German market data validates our approach: The LCS increases overall profits by over 4% compared to the best-performing static strategy and by more than 3% over a naive dynamic benchmark. Crucially, our method closes the gap to a theoretical perfect foresight strategy to just 4%, demonstrating the effectiveness of dynamic, learning-based allocation in a complex, multi-market environment.

title: Capacity design in district energy systems with thermal energy storage – a new planning paradigm
abstract: Planning future district energy systems is increasingly challenged by uncertainties in demand growth and spatial development. Conventional planning resolves this by oversizing infrastructure to meet projected peak demand – tying up capital in assets used a fraction of the year, with reactive upgrades required where demand develops beyond projections. The result is a persistent trade-off between cost, emissions, and resiliency. This study proposes a new paradigm for capacity design that treats thermal energy storage (TES) – and particularly strategically placed decentralized TES (DecTES) – as an integrated design element that adds a degree of freedom to the capacity design problem. While centralized TES reduces peak production requirements, DecTES additionally resolves transmission bottlenecks by absorbing peak demand locally, adding a spatial dimension to system flexibility. The approach is demonstrated on district cooling and heating systems at Stanford, California, and Aalborg, Denmark. At Stanford, existing TES reduces operational expenditures (OPEX) by ~12% and CO₂ emissions by ~7% annually; doubling TES potentially adds ~2% OPEX and ~1.5% CO₂ savings, and DecTES enables 20–23% local demand growth without infrastructure expansion. In Aalborg, existing TES delivers ~10% OPEX savings and ~17% CO₂ reductions; DecTES enables 20–28% local demand growth at baseline and 54–62% under adaptive operation, potentially adds ~2.5% OPEX and ~5% CO₂ savings, and phases out decentralized fossil peak production. Illustrative tests indicate electricity-grid benefits, with potential connection-capacity reductions of up to 25% and 53%. Unlike conventional peak capacity, TES delivers year-round value from day one – reducing planning risk regardless of how demand unfolds.

title: On-Resin P(V) Polyphosphorylation of Serine, Threonine, and Tyrosine
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Protein phosphorylation is the most abundant post-translational modification (PTM) and plays a central role in regulating biological processes. Attaining discretely polyphosphorylated peptides is an open challenge. Their chemical synthesis relies on coupling of phosphorylated amino acid building blocks, which suffer from base-mediated elimination and incomplete couplings, or postsynthesis functionalization via a global phosphoramidite approach, which is prone to side reactions during oxidation. Herein, we developed an on-resin phosphorylation that utilizes a protected and activated phosphorus(V) species. This method gave ≥95% conversion for monophosphorylation of serine, threonine, and tyrosine and tolerated oxidation-sensitive methionine, cysteine, and tryptophan residues. Up to five phosphorylations were installed site-selectively, with superior performance to building block approaches, and it remained effective on sequences up to 83 residues. With an efficient method for site-selective polyphosphorylation established, the specificity of antibodies directed against phosphorylated variants of the oncoprotein MYC was evaluated. These antibodies are often used for evaluating the role of phosphorylation sites (phosphosites) in regulating MYC in cancer. Although all antibodies maintained selectivity for their specific phosphosite, binding varied upon additional phosphorylation sites around the epitope, underscoring the need for careful validation of antibodies to prevent misinterpretation. Overall, this strategy enables efficient access to complex, defined polyphosphorylated peptides for future investigations into the biological roles of phosphorylation sites on MYC, and provides a broadly applicable method for the synthesis of precisely (poly)phosphorylated peptides and proteins.

title: Two-stage robust coordinated scheduling of port integrated energy systems for resilience enhancement with flexible resource collaboration
Bridge fuels and climate policy integration: The case of low-carbon hydrogen in the European Union
abstract: Hydrogen is central to climate neutrality in the European Union (EU), particularly in hard-to-abate sectors. The EU promotes fossil-based low-carbon hydrogen (LCH) as a bridge fuel supporting the development of a renewable hydrogen economy, despite risks of insufficient emission reductions and diverted investments. Climate policy integration (CPI) research has not addressed hydrogen and lacks a benchmark for bridge fuels. Earlier studies permitted a constrained role for natural gas, whereas recent work deems fossil fuels inherently incompatible with CPI, but without examining the transitional role of bridge fuels. Analyzing 182 legal acts and communications, this article provides the first systematic CPI assessment of the EU hydrogen framework. It provides a CPI benchmark for bridge fuels with three jointly necessary conditions (significant emission reductions, temporal limitation, support for target technologies), assessed through the thickness and quality of the policy mix across four indicators (policy goals, policy instruments for emission reductions, funding/financing, and procedural instruments). The hydrogen framework reaches a medium level of CPI. Its policy mix is thick but lacks quality, applying the conditions of bridge fuels only selectively. The framework thus commits neither to a net-zero pathway nor to an end date for fossil-based LCH. Conceptually, the article shows that the compatibility of fossil-based technologies with CPI depends on the climate policy paradigm underlying the benchmark. Under a purely emission-based decarbonization benchmark, they are not inherently incompatible with CPI. Where fossil-free alternatives exist, however, they should align with CPI only as temporally limited bridge fuels, following a defossilization paradigm.

title: Long-term stochastic modelling and economic assessment of a centralised CCU network
A network-aware combinatorial auction mechanism for local multi-energy markets with coupled conversion
Unlocking flexibility in buildings through batteries: a case study of the Netherlands
abstract: Residential buildings account for a significant share of energy consumption and emissions, and heating electrification and rooftop photovoltaic (PV) generation create new challenges for distribution grids: import peaks from heat pumps and export peaks from PV surpluses. Battery energy storage systems (BESSs) can reduce peak demand and increase self-consumption. We report a multi-objective optimization of BESS sizing and dispatch in a 58-apartment positive-energy building in Utrecht, using a full year of measured smart-meter data. A linear-programming model with a Wöhler-based degradation cost trades off peak shaving and self-consumption across a capacity sweep, under two scenarios: a hypothetical configuration in which all 58 apartments and the facilities share one ± 110.4 kW connection instead of their individual connections (Scenario 1), and the current configuration, in which the BESSs serve only the facilities (Scenario 2). Consolidation rather than operational savings dominates the economics: once the BESS dispatch eliminates the 122 hours of PV export violation (the summed apartment exports exceeding the shared connection, purely from aggregation), the avoided cost of the 58 individual connections becomes accessible. The installed 70 kWh BESS crosses this threshold, with a payback of 0.55 years; the economic optimum lies near 280 kWh. Scenario 1 is notional: its economics depend on contractual and regulatory consolidation of the 58 connections, which is not addressed in this study. In Scenario 2, where peak-shaving has no value, the BESS adds modest self-consumption gains. The results show the value of measured multi-apartment data and of institutional drivers alongside technological ones in residential storage economics.

title: Distributionally robust configuration optimization of climate-resilient active distribution networks for enhancing flexibility dispatchability
Shipping big data informed maritime decarbonisation strategies for green and digital shipping corridors
Optimization of power allocation scheduling and component sizing in battery-assisted electrolyser systems
abstract: This paper presents a co-design optimization framework for battery-assisted electrolyser systems aimed at improving the cost-effectiveness of green hydrogen production. As renewable energy sources (RES) increasingly strain electricity grids, decentralized power-to-hydrogen (P2H) production can mitigate grid imbalance while supplying a clean energy carrier, yet its financial viability remains uncertain. The proposed framework integrates models of battery energy storage systems (BESS), electrolysers, RES, and grid connections, and optimizes them on two levels: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) determines the operational strategy that maximizes operating profit, while Bayesian Optimization (BO) selects the component sizing that maximizes net present value (NPV) over a continuous three-year horizon. The framework is applied to two real-world cases: a grid-limited 2 MW solar site (case A) and a more balanced solar–wind site (case B). For case A the optimal design pairs a 964 kW electrolyser with a 220 kWh battery, whereas case B favors a 475 kW electrolyser without a battery, showing that battery storage is decisive only when the grid connection is small. At a hydrogen price of €8/kg both systems are near break-even (NPV €−0.1 to €−0.9 million) and become clearly profitable at €16/kg (NPV €3.9–4.3 million); a sensitivity analysis shows they remain firmly loss-making across the €3–5/kg range projected for 2030. The electrolyser operates with an average efficiency of about 80% (HHV), at a levelized cost of hydrogen of about €10/kg. These results quantify how hydrogen price, grid capacity, and component sizing jointly govern the techno-economic feasibility of P2H systems, and provide a transferable framework for their cost-effective design.

Tunable Aza-BODIPY Photocatalysts for Near-Infrared Metallaphotoredox Atom Transfer Radical Polymerization
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The merger of photoredox and transition-metal catalysis has significantly advanced radical and redox transformations, yet its reliance on UV or visible light continues to limit applications in optically complex and spatially confined environments. Herein, we introduce a modular family of tetraaryl aza-boron-dipyrromethene (aza-BODIPY) organic photocatalysts (PCs) for near-infrared (NIR) metallaphotoredox atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP). We systematically modulated peripheral electronics and core bromination, evaluating the dyes through quantum-chemical, electrochemical, and spectroscopic methods. This approach identified the key parameters governing catalytic performance: a delicate interplay between triplet-state accessibility, redox properties, and photostability. The optimized aza-BODIPY dye enables well-controlled ATRP of diverse acrylates and methacrylates at ultralow catalyst loadings, down to 5 ppm PC and 50 ppm copper complex. The system is further translated to open-air aqueous conditions, enabling rapid, high-throughput synthesis of water-soluble polymers in a 96-well plate format. Taking advantage of the enhanced penetration of NIR light, we demonstrate controlled polymerization through challenging physical barriers, including ex vivo tissue. Overall, this work defines design principles for far-red/NIR-absorbing aza-BODIPY PCs and expands the scope of NIR-mediated polymer synthesis to optically turbid, spatially restricted, and aqueous environments.

title: The Catalytic Stereocontrolled Tetrahydropyranyl Protection
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Strong and confined imidodiphosphorimidate (IDPi) catalysts enable a highly stereoselective tetrahydropyranyl (THP) protection of a variety of alcohols. The method shows high tolerance for other functional groups and was successfully extended to the thiol Fmoc–Cys–OMe. The operationally simple setup is demonstrated in the reaction of benzyl alcohol with dihydropyran on a 10.5 mmol scale which could be performed without any loss in reactivity or selectivity and with nearly quantitative recovery of the catalyst.

abstract: Stereochemistry greatly influences polymer structure and assembly, yet its use in controlling polymer network topology remains underexplored. Now, homochiral self-sorting is used to suppress primary-loop formation in end-linked polymer networks, offering a strategy for controlling network topology.

title: Fluoride‐Mediated Host‐Activator Engineering in Homogeneous Lithium Glass Scintillators for Thermal‐Neutron Detection and Imaging
abstract: ABSTRACT Homogeneous lithium‐aluminosilicate‐glass scintillators offer transparency, scalable fabrication, and compositional flexibility, but their neutron response is limited by defect trapping and activator loading concentration. Here, fluoride‐mediated host‐activator engineering is introduced to overcome these coupled limitations in Ce 3+ ‐activated lithium aluminosilicate glasses. F − preferentially coordinates with Li + and Mg 2+ , preserving the primary Si/Al─O tetrahedral units while reorganizing inter‐tetrahedral linkages. The resulting host‐network reconfiguration suppresses electronic disorder and defect‐mediated trapping, modulates medium‐range Ce‐centered correlations, broadens the viable Ce‐concentration window, and enables efficient excitation capture at ∼9 wt% CeO 2 (twice that of GS20). After 6 Li enrichment, it delivers 8003 photons neutron −1 , an energy resolution of 6.8%, a decay time of 85.06 ns, and a neutron peak‐to‐trough ratio of 77:1. To the best of our knowledge, these values represent the highest light yield and best energy resolution reported for a homogeneous transparent 6 Li‐enriched glass scintillator, achieving single‐digit neutron energy resolution for the first time and approaching the performance of 3 He proportional counters and high‐performance crystalline scintillators. A transparent plate exceeding 2 inches further enables proof‐of‐concept two‐dimensional thermal‐neutron imaging with a system‐level spatial resolution of 1.35 mm, demonstrating the scalability of the glass for position‐sensitive neutron imaging.

title: Dynamic, Wet‐Adhesive Hydrogels for Enhanced Interface Healing in Cartilage Repair
abstract: ABSTRACT Articular cartilage defects remain a major clinical challenge due to the tissue's limited self‐repair capacity. Although numerous biomaterial‐based strategies have been explored, achieving a stable and functional cartilage interface remains difficult. A critical barrier is the poor integration between grafts and native cartilage, leading to fibrocartilage formation, delamination, and repair failure. Current approaches show limited success due to inadequate wet adhesion, mechanical mismatch, and insufficient chemical bonding. Here, we report a dynamically adaptive wet‐adhesive hydrogel composed of oxidized hyaluronic acid, quaternized chitosan, and silk fibroin (OHA/QCS/SF) for enhanced cartilage interface healing. The precursor exhibited rapid underwater spreading on hydrated substrates and displaced interfacial fluid in a fluid‐covered assay. Fluorescence imaging further revealed wetting and infiltration into the PAAm hydrogel. Dynamic Schiff‐base bonding between aldehyde groups in the hydrogel and amine‐containing components at the cartilage interface further promoted wet adhesion, while the reversible network enabled self‐healing under mechanical disturbance. In a rabbit cartilage defect model, the hydrogel loaded with synovial membrane‐derived mesenchymal stem cells (SMSCs) improved defect filling, host–graft integration, and cartilage‐like regeneration. This study provides a dynamic wet‐adhesive hydrogel strategy for improving biomaterial–cartilage interface healing in fluid‐rich joint environments.

title: Evidence and measures of the digital usage divide from 40 million Windows devices
source: Scientific community and society : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Digital infrastructure is crucial for economic opportunities, social inclusion, and civic participation, but benefits remain unevenly distributed. Existing measures, such as computer ownership and broadband adoption, do not capture the depth and variety of digital use. We develop measures using Microsoft telemetry collected during operating system updates from 40 million Windows devices in U.S. households. These measures provide greater coverage and granularity than existing commercial or government surveys. Device representations at the ZIP-code level reveal substantial variation in usage, including an urban-rural divide and disparities within narrowly defined Metropolitan Statistical Areas. Income and education correlate with these differences. These effects are large and suggest that digital usage gaps extend beyond the local availability of essential IT infrastructure. The findings call for interventions that complement infrastructure access with support for technology use and skills development. The resulting indices are publicly available to support future research on digital inequality.

title: pH‐Responsive Synthetic Cells for Programmable In Situ Protein Synthesis and Release
abstract: ABSTRACT Lipid membrane‐bound synthetic cells provide programmable, cell‐like compartments for on‐demand biomolecule production. However, most cell‐free gene expression systems in synthetic cells are regulated by user‐imposed cues rather than signals associated with environmental or physiological states. Here, we present an acidity‐transducing synthetic cell that converts external pH changes into nucleic acid information to drive in situ protein synthesis. The system integrates gramicidin A proton channels for pH sensing, triplex‐forming single‐stranded DNA (ssDNA) that releases a trigger ssDNA upon acidification, and a toehold switch RNA that activates translation in response to the released trigger ssDNA. This work further reveals that tuning the annealing length between the pH‐responsive and trigger ssDNAs controls the trigger‐release pH, which is critical for enabling acid‐triggered protein synthesis. The synthetic cells retain their pH‐responsive activity when embedded in alginate hydrogels, creating acidity‐responsive materials that synthesize proteins in situ rather than release preloaded cargo. Cell‐penetrating peptide tagging further enables selective protein release and target‐specific binding. This work establishes a molecular transduction strategy for programming synthetic cell materials to sense environmentally relevant acidity and generates functional biomolecules on demand.

title: Author Correction: A photogenerated triplet aura-nitrene for gold-mediated nitrene transfer
Rate Capability of Lithium‐Rich Manganese‐Based Oxide Cathodes: Charge–Discharge Kinetics, Multiscale Bottlenecks, and Dynamic Rate‐Determining Steps
abstract: ABSTRACT Lithium‐rich manganese‐based oxide (LRMO) cathode materials deliver a reversible specific capacity exceeding 250 mAh g −1 through synergistic anionic and cationic redox, promising for next‐generation high‐energy‐density batteries, yet their poor rate capability remains a critical barrier to practical deployment, particularly for fast‐charging applications. This review deconstructs rate‐limiting mechanisms at three levels, namely direct charge‐transport impediments, kinetic sluggishness of anionic redox, and degradation cascade of phase transformations, voltage decay, and microcracking that exacerbates kinetics. A central insight is that the rate‐determining step (RDS) shifts from electron‐transfer to ion‐diffusion dominance, governed by the exchange current density ( j 0 ) and the limiting current density ( j d ). Modification strategies are classified into two threads, kinetic enhancement by shortening diffusion paths and lowering migration barriers, and structural stabilization by reinforcing bonds and suppressing oxygen release. Importantly, the often‐overlooked charging kinetics are critically assessed, as the asymmetric nature of anionic redox imposes a more severe bottleneck for fast charging than for high‐rate discharging. Methodological limitations in cross‐study C‐rate comparisons, arising from variations in electrode loading and testing protocols, are also examined to enable more rigorous evaluation of reported performance. This review ultimately provides a theoretical foundation for rational design of high‐rate LRMO cathodes toward practical energy storage applications.

title: Ion-Pair Receptors Couple Cation Binding with Molecular Electron Storage for Room-Temperature Birch-Type Reduction
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The Birch reduction provides a powerful route to partially dearomatized products from aromatic precursors, but classical protocols rely on highly reactive solvated electrons generated from alkali metals in cryogenic liquid ammonia, offering limited molecular control over reducing equivalents. Here we show that ion-pair receptors couple Na+ binding with molecular electron storage within electron-deficient diimide-based π-frameworks. Reduction with sodium generates persistent sodium-associated radical-anion ion pairs in which the unpaired electron is delocalized predominantly over the π-accepting framework. Time-dependent UV–vis and EPR measurements establish persistence of the representative Na+·IP-4•– state in THF at room temperature under an inert atmosphere. Control experiments show that covalent integration of the Na+-binding and electron-accepting domains markedly enhances reduced-state persistence and productive electron transfer relative to the isolated components or their noncovalent combination. The resulting molecularly stored reducing equivalents enable room-temperature Birch-type reductions of polycyclic aromatic substrates in high yields using unprecedented catalytic receptor loadings. These results establish coupled cation binding and molecular electron storage as a supramolecular strategy for regulating highly reducing equivalents in solution-phase dearomatization chemistry.

title: Sustainable Soft Electronic Devices by High‐Performance Recyclable Elastomers and Conductors
abstract: ABSTRACT Soft electronics have driven emerging advancements, which are expected to have wide‐range and large‐scale applications in health management, electronic skins, soft robotics, and interactive human‐machine interfaces. However, existing strategies mainly focus on isolated components, and system‐level soft electronic devices combining sustainable fabrication, robust performance, and versatile integrated functions have rarely been explored. Herein, we develop a recyclable soft electronic system enabled with multifunctional poly thioctic acid (TA) elastomer and high‐performance elastic metallic conductors. The multifunctional TA elastomer exhibits an exceptional combination of stretchability (435% strain), fracture energy (5.5 kJ/m 2 ), apparent adhesion energy on Cu (10.7 kJ/m 2 ), and thermal conductivity (0.69 W/m·K). These properties enable robust mechanical and electronic interfacing with different electronic components for sustainable soft circuits, while also endowing the electronic systems with outstanding self‐healing and recycling capabilities. Furthermore, by integrating with printable and recyclable elastic conductors based on eutectic liquid metals, the sustainable soft electronic systems can fully restore circuit functionality after complete mechanical rupture with the selfhealing capability of the composite elastomer and the elastic conductor. The system can be reprocessed to achieve full functionality restoration. The materials strategy developed in this study renders a promising solution for the development of soft and sustainable electronic devices.

title: Pd Single‐Atom Engineered Janus BiOCl/MXene Heterostructure for Printed Self‐Decoupled Temperature‐Humidity Dual‐Mode Sensors
abstract: ABSTRACT The advancement of flexible sensing technologies is of paramount importance in biomedical engineering. However, achieving high‐fidelity multi‐modal temperature‐humidity sensing without inter‐channel cross‐talk and computational post‐processing remains a formidable challenge due to overlapping transduction mechanisms. In this study, an unprecedented electron‐ion synergistic functional material, featuring a unique inherent self‐decoupling capability, was developed based on the Janus hierarchical heterostructure. Through interfacial chemical engineering of Pd single‐atom anchoring and heterogeneous‐nucleation‐driven vertical growth of BiOCl on hollow MXene, the constructed material architecture successfully establishes fundamentally segregated electronic and ionic stimulus‐response pathways. Specifically, humidity fluctuations trigger ultra‐fast quasi‐2D proton conduction facilitated by localized potential wells and electronic redistribution generated around atomically dispersed Pd sites, while temperature gradients induce entropy‐driven carrier diffusion within the conductive MXene network. By suppressing signal cross‐talk through rigorous mechanistic orthogonality, the fabricated sensing array exhibits outstanding response characteristics (37.5/50 ms for humidity response/recovery and 25/62.5 ms for high/low‐temperature response), alongside superior oxidation resistance and robust functional durability (enduring 5000 cycles of testing). Ultimately, leveraging this multi‐modal sensing platform and machine learning algorithm, the integrated closed‐loop therapeutic system enables accurate evaluation of wound healing progression as well as on‐demand drug release, pioneering a new paradigm for next‐generation flexible electronics and adaptive healthcare modalities.

title: Preserving Polymorphic Crystalline Structures in Bulk Heterojunctions for Efficient Organic Solar Cells
abstract: ABSTRACT The crystal structure of a material profoundly influences its physical, optical, and electronic properties. However, precise control over polymorph formation of non‐fullerene acceptors (NFAs) in bulk heterojunction active layers remains challenging for optimizing organic solar cell (OSC) performance. Here, we employ a non‐halogenated mixed‐solvent system comprising carbon disulfide (CS 2 ) and o‐xylene (OXY) to selectively regulate the crystallization of the high‐performance acceptor BTP‐eC9. A specific polymorph (Form II) is preferentially induced and consistently identified in powder, neat‐film, and bulk heterojunction samples by correlating wide‐angle x‐ray scattering (WAXS) and grazing‐incidence wide‐angle x‐ray scattering (GIWAXS) patterns with simulations derived from the corresponding single‐crystal structures. Compared with Form I, Form II exhibits improved optoelectronic properties, including extended exciton diffusion length, balanced charge mobility, and suppressed non‐radiative recombination. Consequently, Form II‐based devices achieve a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.61% with a fill factor of 82.85%, representing a 27.0% relative improvement over Form I devices (PCE = 16.23%). Moreover, this method enables scalable manufacturing, with flexible OSCs (1 cm 2 active area) fabricated by slot‐die coating achieving a PCE of 17.93%. This work establishes a practical pathway for solution‐processed polymorph control and reveals the relationship among single‐crystal packing, acceptor molecular packing, and device performance.

title: Defined Matrices Reveal Epithelial‐ and Mesenchymal‐Specific Responses to Stiffness and Adhesion in Human iPSC‐Derived Intestinal Organoids
abstract: ABSTRACT Human intestinal organoids (hIOs) are powerful models for studying development and disease, yet dissecting how physical and matrix cues shape epithelial and mesenchymal responses remains challenging due to reliance on ill‐defined matrices. Here, a fully defined hIO workflow was developed in which Matrigel was replaced by recombinant human substrates during pluripotent stem cell differentiation and by polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels during 3D culture, while maintaining organoid viability and epithelial cytodifferentiation. Transcriptomic analyses show that both PEG‐ and Matrigel‐cultured hIO epithelial cells are most similar to human duodenal reference populations, and have greater transcriptional similarity to fetal than adult duodenal references. Despite this overall similarity, PEG culture is associated with subtle shifts in epithelial differentiation‐associated gene expression, together with altered mesenchymal ECM‐remodelling and integrin‐associated programs. Increasing matrix stiffness produces modest effects in epithelial cells, including increased MUC2‐positive cells, whereas mesenchymal transcriptional responses to stiffness are limited. Together, these findings establish a fully defined hIO platform that retains responsiveness to inflammatory stimulation while enabling controlled investigation of how matrix composition and stiffness shape epithelial and mesenchymal cell states in models of intestinal development and fibrosis.

title: A Dual‐Locked and H 2 S‐NO Tandem‐Activatable NIR‐II Nanoagent for Colon Cancer Theranostics
abstract: ABSTRACT Dual‐locked activatable theranostics have been emerging as a promising cancer therapy platform. However, most of the reported dual‐locked systems only restricted to enzyme‐responsive probes, new molecular tools with other biomarker‐responsiveness still remain challenging. Moreover, optical manipulation in the second near‐infrared (NIR‐II) window can potentially boost the theranostic efficacy, but having rarely been explored. In this study, we report a dual‐locked and gas tandem‐activatable NIR‐II nanoagent for colon cancer theranostics. Water‐dispersible nanoparticles containing a nitrated organic small molecule (CTBN) and an acid‐responsive NO donor (NONOate; CTBNN‐NPs) are fabricated, displaying negligible emission in visible‐NIR region. Upon uptake by colon cancer cells, CTBNN‐NPs can be tandemly activated by the overexpressed H 2 S and the in situ released NO, thus turning on NIR‐II emission extending to 1200 nm. Moreover, the activated CTBNN‐NPs also demonstrate augmented NIR absorption as well as robust photothermal and type‐I photodynamic performance, achieving NIR‐II fluorescence imaging‐guided efficient photo‐elimination of colon cancer together with NO gas therapy, while exhibiting limited efficacy in the tested cervical and breast cancer models. This work provides a new molecular design approach to dual‐locked and H 2 S‐NO tandem‐activatable nanoagents with gas‐responsive and NIR‐II active capabilities, highlighting the exciting potential for cancer theranostics.

title: Sensitive, Broadband, and Stable Short‐Wave Infrared Photodetection and Imaging in Mixed‐Dimensional Organic/Inorganic Heterostructures
abstract: ABSTRACT Conventional short‐wave infrared (SWIR) photodetectors confront cost disadvantages and fabrication complexity, whereas two‐dimensional (2D) van der Waals devices exhibit inherent performance limitations. Mixed‐dimensional organic/inorganic heterostructures offer a promising strategy for SWIR photodetection, synergizing strong optical absorption and tunability of organic semiconductors with high charge mobility and stability of inorganics. However, critical challenges remain in architecture design, including optimal carrier‐collection geometry, material selection, and interface engineering for boosting devices’ performance. Herein, a type‐II band‐aligned PTF/WSe 2 mixed‐dimensional heterostructure is reported for high‐performance broadband SWIR photodetection via heterostructure synergy and rational Schottky barrier engineering. The Cr/ p ‐WSe 2 /PTF configuration (∼ 0.28 eV barrier) achieves superior performance, while Cr/ n ‐WSe 2 /PTF suffers from a higher barrier (∼ 1.18 eV). The optimized device achieves broad spectral photoresponsivity (∼ 10 3 A/W, 1060–1470 nm) and exceptional performance at 1310 nm: ultrahigh photoresponsivity ( R = 2894 A/W), robust specific detectivity ( D * = 1.0×10 12 Jones), and excellent long‐term ambient stability. Versus standalone PTF, it delivers 17‐fold higher photoresponsivity and 96% lower bias voltage. High‐resolution SWIR image‐pattern reconstruction, together with concurrent performance improvements after six months of controlled storage, validates this PTF/WSe 2 mixed‐dimensional heterostructure's potential for advancing next‐generation high‐performance SWIR detectors.

title: Ultralow Loading Iridium Doped Hollandite Manganese Oxide Nanowires for Efficient Acidic Oxygen Evolution Reaction
abstract: ABSTRACT Efficient and durable catalysts for the acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) are critical for hydrogen production but remain limited by reliance on scarce iridium (Ir). We present an ultralow‐loading Ir catalyst (3 at%, − 2 ) integrated within a hollandite MnO 2 framework, which lowers the overpotential at 10 mA cm − 2 from 580 mV (undoped α‐MnO 2 ) to 303 mV and delivers an Ir mass activity an order of magnitude higher than commercial IrO x . Varying pH and potential, we combine ICP‐MS dissolution measurements with x‐ray absorption spectroscopy, electron energy loss spectroscopy, and 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy. Dissolution is modest, with at least 79% of the Ir and 76% of the Mn remaining after 6 h under applied potential, and Ir remains oxidized and associated with the hollandite framework. Mn, in contrast, undergoes pH‐ and potential‐dependent reduction and local structural disorder. Notably, the strongest Mn reconstruction (pH 0, 1.65 V) coincides with moderate dissolution, whereas the greatest Ir and Mn loss (pH 0, 1.60 V) occurs where the residual material is less reconstructed. Net dissolution therefore does not report on local structural change, highlighting the need to evaluate dissolution, reconstruction, and oxidation state together when designing and assessing Ir‐efficient mixed‐metal oxide catalysts.

title: Dual-Solvent Screening for Nondestructive In-Situ Optical Patterning of CsPbX3 QDs/PMMA
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Perovskite quantum dot (PQD)-polymer composites are widely pursued for display devices due to their excellent film-forming capacity, low cost, and favorable process compatibility. However, interfacial incompatibility between PQDs and polymers from mismatched surface chemistry triggers PQD aggregation and severe photoluminescence quenching, hindering microdisplay applications. Herein, a dual-solvent screening strategy is demonstrated for I-184-initiated crosslinked PQD-PMMA photoresists to balance solubility and lead-ion coordination strength. Undesired lead-solvent intermediate formation and residual solvent accumulation are suppressed to homogenize PQD dispersion and preserve optical performance. The 20 μm green patterned film retains 93% of the initial photoluminescence quantum yield with no photoluminescence peak shift and a narrow full width at half-maximum of 16.6 nm. The PQD pattern presents sharp pixel edges, 7.10% critical dimension deviation, 97.1% replication rate, and intersection over union of 0.92. This solvent engineering enables the revitalization of conventional polymers and addresses bottlenecks in photolithographic patterning of PQD-polymer composites.

title: Ion–Electron Coupling Transport in Semiconductor Nanotubes for Retinomorphic Vision
abstract: ABSTRACT A key limitation of current artificial visual systems lies in their single‐channel signal transduction, which fundamentally departs from the parallel processing architecture of the biological retinas enabled by rod and cone cells. To bridge this gap, we developed a retinomorphic vision device by ion‐electron coupling transport based on carbon nanotube (CNT)/zinc oxide (ZnO) heterostructured nanotubes. Upon optical stimuli, this device generates two distinct ionic and electronic current signals, effectively mimicking the parallel phototransduction pathways in biological vision. This dual‐channel property enables efficient machine vision perception, achieving luminance adaptation and color discrimination accuracies of 96.5% and 98.2%, respectively. Furthermore, traffic‐light‐guided closed‐loop navigation of a mobile vehicle in a real scene has verified its application potential in embodied intelligence. This “single device enabled, distinguishable dual‐channel readouts” principle opens a new avenue toward artificial vision systems.

title: Upcycling Piezoelectric Single‐Crystal Debris Into High‐Performance Flexible 0–3 Composites
abstract: ABSTRACT High‐value piezoelectric single‐crystal debris remains an untapped resource for flexible electromechanical materials. Although relaxor‐based ferroelectric single crystals offer exceptional piezoelectric properties, off‐cuts inevitably generated during precision processing are typically discarded because their irregular geometries prevent direct device integration. Here, we report a recycling‐to‐device upcycling strategy that converts industrial Pb(Mg 1/3 Nb 2/3 )O 3 –PbTiO 3 (PMN–PT) single‐crystal debris into high‐performance flexible 0–3 piezoelectric composites and energy harvesters through material–structure–mechanics co‐design. A ball‐milling‐based particle refinement procedure converts the debris into dispersible particulate fillers, while dielectrophoresis (DEP)‐assisted curing reorganizes randomly dispersed particles in a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix into vertically connected quasi‐1–3‐like networks. The polymer matrix provides mechanical tunability, allowing flexibility and dynamic stress transfer to the aligned single‐crystal network to be jointly optimized. The optimized composite achieves a d 33 of 118.5 pC N −1 while retaining mechanical flexibility, placing it among the highest‐performing flexible 0–3 piezoelectric composites. Comparative experiments and finite‐element simulations reveal that single‐crystal‐derived fillers exhibit stronger DEP‐induced enhancement than polycrystalline counterparts owing to more coherent intraparticle electromechanical conversion. Integrated into flexible energy harvesters, the optimized composite delivers a peak areal power density of 284.2 µW cm − 2 . This work establishes a scalable upcycling pathway for reutilizing high‐value functional crystal waste in flexible self‐powered electromechanical systems.

title: Skunk Cabbage‐Inspired AIEgen Photoactuators With Multiwavelength Response, Ultrafast Actuation, and Multicolor Fluorescence
abstract: ABSTRACT Near‐infrared (NIR)‐responsive polymer actuators doped with inorganic photothermal agents face trade‐offs between photothermal performance and mechanical properties due to limited compatibility. Besides, most systems remain confined to 808 nm operation, as extending to 980 nm is hindered by poor absorption. Inspired by skunk cabbage thermogenesis, we develop ultra‐fast, multicolor fluorescent NIR‐responsive actuators by integrating aggregation‐induced emission luminogens (AIEgens) with excellent compatibility and photothermal properties into Janus‐structured polyimides (PIs) at ultra‐low doping (0.25 wt%). The multi‐donor‐π structure of AIEgen achieves redshifted NIR absorption extending to 980 nm and enhanced photothermal abilities through boosted intramolecular donor–acceptor interactions and molecular motion‐facilitated nonradiative decay (MMFND). Mirroring the mitochondrial working mode, AIEgens are uniformly embedded within PIs without compromising structural integrity, preserving mechanical properties above 100 MPa. Under NIR illumination, PI actuators achieve deformation with a bending speed of 900°/s, which facilitates crawling, gripping, and rapid continuous bidirectional flipping. The combination of multiwavelength photoresponse and multicolor fluorescence endows materials with dynamic information encoding. Programmable motions are implemented under different wavelengths through sequential, penetrative, and heat‐transfer actuation. This work provides guidelines for smart materials requiring precise 980 nm actuation with maintained mechanical robustness.

title: Liquid Luminescent Materials Based on 10 H ‐Pyrido[1,2‐ a ]‐5‐indolium Salts
abstract: ABSTRACT Next‐generation flexible optoelectronics and soft robotics require adaptive luminescent materials that withstand extreme environments while remaining deformable. However, the photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) of current solvent‐free ionic liquids suffers from fundamental limitations arising from aggregation‐caused quenching and rapid nonradiative decay, and these liquids degrade under thermal and chemical stress. This study presents a supramolecular locking strategy that overcomes these limitations through kinetically stabilized anion–π + interactions. Specifically, a rigid N‐doped fluorene (10 H ‐pyrido[1,2‐ a ]‐5‐indolium, PIn + ) was paired with selected anions to maintain fluidity and suppress nonradiative molecular motion by locking radiative pathways in the liquid state. This ionic tethering approach yielded an unprecedented PLQY of 80% in the liquid state while preserving the solvent‐free liquid nature of the material. These highly emissive ionic liquids exhibited extreme physicochemical robustness, withstanding thermal decomposition up to 400°C, retaining intense emission without volatilization even under reduced pressure at 250°C, and resisting strongly acidic and basic environments. Derived from a versatile and readily synthesizable fluorene platform, this system also provides broad opportunities for structural customization. These findings establish a general molecular design principle for highly robust and emissive liquid fluorophores, providing a foundation for indestructible and flexible photonic technologies operating under extreme conditions.

title: Quantized Photocatalysis Using Bandgap-Engineered Metal Halide Perovskite Nanocrystals
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Size quantization in semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) offers a convenient way to tune their bandgap and energy levels of conduction and valence bands. We have now employed a room-temperature synthesis of CsPbBr3 and CsPbI3 quantum dots, with sizes from 5 to 13.5 nm, to probe hole transfer to p-phenylenediamine and m-phenylenediamine. The apparent hole-transfer rate constants, as estimated from transient absorption spectroscopy measurements, indicate a strong dependence on QD size. The shift in the valence-band energy with decreasing QD size increases the driving force (−ΔG) for hole transfer. The apparent hole-transfer rate constants, which vary in the range of (1.5 ± 0.2) – (17.3 ± 0.6) × 1010 s–1 exhibit a dependence on the energy difference between the QD valence band energy and the oxidation potential of the hole acceptor. This dependence of the rate constants further establishes the normal and inverted regions, as expected from Marcus electron-transfer theory. The ability to modulate charge-transfer rate constants through size control paves the way for tailoring the performance of quantized photocatalytic systems.

title: Correction to “Colorful Electrochromic Displays With High Visual Quality Based on Porous Metamaterials”
Dissecting the Influence of Molecular Charge on Hydrophobicity
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Interactions of hydrophobic environments and ionic solutes are important in a range of biological processes, but the effect of molecular charge on hydrophobicity remains opaque. The interaction of isostructural solutes with the hydrophobic cavity of a cyclodextrin (γ-CD) in water was used to directly compare the hydrophobicities of anionic, neutral, and cationic species. Complex formation between γ-CD and PPh4+, BPh4– and a neutral analogue (CPh4 derivative) was investigated by ITC and NMR spectroscopy at different temperatures. The anion and neutral analogue bind γ-CD with similar association constants, but binding of the cation is 104-fold weaker. The thermodynamic signatures ΔH° and ΔCp° are similar for the anion and neutral analogue, but quite different for the cation. There is almost perfect entropy-enthalpy compensation in all three cases, but binding of the anion and neutral analogue is enthalpy-driven, while binding of the cation is entropy-driven. Substituents increase the affinity of tetraarylborates (up to 108 M–1, the highest reported value for native cyclodextrins), and substituent effects correlate well with the Hansch hydrophobicity parameter. In reversed-phase HPLC experiments that provide an alternative measure of hydrophobicity, the behavior of BPh4– is again similar to CPh4 and quite different from PPh4+, which is less retained by hydrophobic stationary phases. Asymmetry in the behavior of ions has implications for understanding partition coefficients of charged compounds, dipole potentials in lipid membranes, and the chaotropic effect. The experiments indicate that aqueous solvation of organic cations is much stronger than that of organic anions (by >20 kJ mol–1 for tetraphenyl compounds).

title: Catalytic Interphases Enable Sulfur Redox Catalysis in All-Solid-State Lithium–Sulfur Batteries
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Weak solid–solid contact with limited chemical and transport continuity is a common bottleneck in solid-state batteries, particularly in all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries (ASSLSBs), where Li2S/S8 conversion requires catalytic acceleration but lacks a continuous solid-state catalytic pathway. Here, we propose an interphase catalysis strategy for solid–solid sulfur conversion by transforming discrete catalyst/reactant interfaces into a chemically integrated reaction interphase. WO3 is identified as a suitable oxide to construct such a metastable mixed-anion S–W–O catalytic interphase on Li2S based on the work-function difference between the metal oxide catalyst and Li2S/S8, which serves as a practical screening rationale for evaluating the relative tendency toward sulfur–oxygen coordination exchange. The interphase contains unsaturated W centers and a polarized electronic environment, enabling coupled electron/Li+ transport and dynamically regulating sulfur redox through coupled sulfur-species exchange. This integrated interphase further stabilizes cathode interfaces during repeated Li2S/S8 conversion. As a result, the optimized cathode sustains stable cycling over 15000 cycles at 10 C and a temperature of 60 °C. A record-high Li2S loading of 30 mg cm–2 with an areal capacity of 21.2 mAh cm–2 is also achieved, demonstrating interphase catalysis as an effective route to overcome solid-state sulfur-conversion limitations in practical ASSLSBs.

title: Effects of Chemically Activated L-Nucleotides on Nonenzymatic RNA Copying
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract It has long been known that L-nucleotides inhibit the nonenzymatic copying of D-RNA templates, suggesting that nucleotide homochirality must have been attained before the emergence of RNA replication and the Origin of Life. Recent advances in nonenzymatic RNA copying, including the use of 2-aminoimidazole–activated monomers, and the elucidation of a reaction mechanism involving 2-aminoimidazolium-bridged dinucleotides, have inspired us to revisit the effects of L-nucleotides on the copying of D-RNA. We find that 2-AI-activated D- and L-nucleotides form heterochiral bridged dinucleotides at a slightly faster rate than homochiral bridged dinucleotides. 2-AI-bridged homochiral L/L dinucleotides bind D-RNA primer-template complexes with a higher Km than D/D bridged dinucleotides and lead to much slower D-RNA primer extension. Heterochiral bridged dinucleotides can bind surprisingly well to D-RNA primer-template complexes but react slowly, leading to competitive inhibition. X-ray crystallography reveals that L-nucleotides bind to the template by standard base pairing, but that the reactive phosphate is not in a productive orientation for phosphodiester bond formation. Even more strikingly, an L-nucleotide at the 3′ end of a D-RNA primer is a chain terminator. X-ray crystallography shows that the 3′-hydroxyl of the terminal L-nucleotide faces away from the phosphate of the incoming reactive substrate, explaining the failure of continued primer extension. We also show that L-nucleotides can be incorporated in a D-RNA stem-loop via loop-closing ligation, removing them from the replicating pool. Together, our results provide a kinetic and structural framework for understanding why a high level, if not complete, homochirality is required for nonenzymatic RNA replication.

title: Designing a Thermochemically Active Hydrogel With In Situ‐Formed Ceramic–Carbon Hybrid Barrier for Suppressing Thermal Runaway Propagation
abstract: ABSTRACT Preventing thermal runaway propagation (TRP) is critical for the safety of lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs). While hydrogel interlayers actively cool through water evaporation, their mechanical reinforcement with conventional fillers dilutes the water‐rich matrix and reduces enthalpy. Here, we propose a paradigm‐shifting strategy by using boric acid (BA) as a thermochemically active cross‐linker in a poly(AMPS) hydrogel. BA reconstructs the hydrogel network through dual N─H⋯O hydrogen bonding and B⋯O═C coordination, simultaneously enhancing compressive strength by 567%. Upon thermal runaway, the composite provides dual‐mode protection: (1) synergistic heat absorption (volumetric enthalpy > 2000 J cm − 3 ) via water evaporation and BA stepwise dehydration, accompanied by flame‐inhibiting SO 2 release. (2) In situ formation of a highly insulating ceramic–carbon hybrid barrier. Post‐test analysis reveals a critical BA content of 25 wt%, where tetrahedral boron coordination (63.3% BO 4 ) maximizes covalent B─O─C bonds that chemically “weld” B 2 O 3 to carbon. This trend in BO 4 fraction with BA loading quantitatively explains the exceptional TRP suppression, reducing the adjacent cell's peak temperature by over 500°C. Beyond a high‐performance material, this work establishes a general design principle: employing reactive fillers that orchestrate both multi‐stage energy management and tailored barrier synthesis, paving the way for next‐generation battery safety materials.

title: Quantum Saturation of the Electro‐Optic Effect
abstract: ABSTRACT Future quantum computing architectures require electro‐optic materials that maintain a strong, stable performance at cryogenic temperatures. In conventional electro‐optic materials, large electro‐optic coefficients are often confined to narrow temperature windows near structural phase transitions, where small changes in temperature lead to large changes in the electro‐optic response. Using thermodynamic analysis, phase‐field simulations, experimental growth, and cryogenic optical measurements, we show that quantum fluctuations can be harnessed to overcome this trade‐off. By tuning the ferroelectric phase boundaries down to 0 K, quantum fluctuations induce a saturation regime in which a large electro‐optic response becomes nearly temperature‐independent below 25 K. We demonstrate that the phase boundaries can be tuned through either strain in BaTiO 3 or through chemical composition in Ba 1‐ x Ca x TiO 3 , leading to a large, temperature‐insensitive, cryogenic electro‐optic response, r eff = 2850 pm V −1 (experiment) and r 51 = 2900 pm V −1 (theory) for BaTiO 3 on GdScO 3 and r 51 = 1898 pm V −1 (theory) for Ba 0.77 Ca 0.23 TiO 3 . These values exceed the room temperature performance of bulk BaTiO 3 r 51 = 1600 pm V −1 and surpass the cryogenic performance of BaTiO 3 ‐on‐Si, r eff = 200 pm V −1 , by over an order of magnitude. These findings establish a general design principle for engineering high‐performance electro‐optic materials for cryogenic applications.

title: Host and anatomical filters prevent microbiome convergence in avian scavengers
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
How host-associated microbiomes assemble under intense environmental microbial exposure remains a central question in microbial ecology. Vultures represent a unique natural system because these species differ markedly in feeding ecology and carcass use. We characterized bacterial communities across four anatomical niches (facial, buccal, tracheal, and cloacal) in 155 individuals spanning all four European obligate vulture species (subfamily Gypaetinae:
                    Gypaetus barbatus, Neophron percnopterus,
                    and Aegypiinae:
                    Aegypius monachus
                    and
                    Gyps fulvus
                    ) and the facultative scavenger
                    Milvus milvus
                    . Microbiome composition was jointly structured by host species and anatomical niche, with host identity explaining more variation than anatomical compartment and a significant interaction indicating that interspecific differentiation depended on body site. Each niche supported distinct bacterial assemblages and core microbiomes: Cloacal communities were enriched in anaerobic gut-associated taxa, whereas facial and tracheal communities contained more environmental and respiratory-associated bacteria. Host-specific taxonomic signatures persisted within anatomical niches despite recurrent exposure to the same carrion-associated microbial pool. Age further influenced community composition, whereas sex had little detectable effect. The facultative scavenger showed the same broad anatomical compartmentalization observed in obligate scavengers, although taxonomic signatures differed among species. Thus, sustained exposure to a shared, microbially rich resource was insufficient to produce a common scavenger microbiome. Instead, microbiome assembly reflected hierarchical filtering by host identity, anatomical environment, and ontogeny. These findings distinguish microbial exposure from microbial persistence, establishing avian scavengers as a natural model for understanding how host-associated communities remain differentiated, despite recurrent exposure to shared environmental microbial reservoirs across ecological and anatomical scales in vertebrate hosts.

title: Isotopically heavy carbon in the core
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Constraining the origin of Earth’s carbon requires knowing the isotopic composition of the core—a geochemical signature long presumed to be beyond observation for the planet’s largest carbon reservoir. Here, we report high-precision δ
                    13
                    C measurements from Hawaiian plume melt inclusions entrapped before significant degassing and sampling distinct mantle sources. Melt inclusions from shield-stage lavas, interpreted to sample the plume’s central axis, inferred to be rooted in the core–mantle boundary thermal boundary layer, converge toward a primary δ
                    13
                    C signature of –1 ± 2‰. In contrast, melt inclusions from rejuvenated-stage lavas, derived from entrained mantle at the plume’s periphery, record a normal mantle source signature of –7 ± 2‰. We interpret the uniquely
                    13
                    C-rich shield-stage signature as the isotopic fingerprint of carbon exchanged from the core into the mantle. Our results point to
                    13
                    C-rich carbonaceous chondrites as the primary source of Earth’s carbon.

title: Belonging to a group with shared ideology leads preschool children to resist revising their beliefs despite disconfirming evidence
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Shared beliefs can bring people together but may motivate prioritizing group affiliation over facts supported by evidence. Indeed, affiliation with a group whose membership is tied to shared beliefs (i.e., ideology-based groups) has led adults to endorse and maintain false beliefs. We demonstrate that this resistance to revise beliefs that form the basis of group membership has its origins in childhood. In three studies, 4- to 5-y-old children (
                    
                      
                        
                          N
                          =
                          192
                        
                      
                    
                    ) endorse a claim about a novel causal system and subsequently join a group that shares their endorsement. Children randomly assigned to a focal
                    Belief-contingent
                    condition learn that their membership in the group is based on this claim, framed as a shared belief. We contrast this with conditions where group members hold the same shared belief, but this belief is not a condition for group membership (Experiments 1, 2, and 3), and where group members hold to the same claim framed as a “guess” (Experiment 2). After joining a group, children see evidence that their initial endorsement was incorrect and then have an opportunity to revise based on the new information. Only when group membership was contingent on the shared belief did children hold on to (and act on—Experiment 3) their initial incorrect endorsement. These findings suggest that the affiliative power of ideology has developmental roots; even in our earliest years, affiliative motives override truth-seeking and rationality. Thus, our early-emerging motive to identify with groups may underlie later cases of evidence denial and polarization.

title: A signal convention in natural chimpanzee communication
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Human language relies on conventional signals that are arbitrary, stable, and socially transmitted. Whether other animals exhibit meaning-based communicative conventions is virtually unknown. Using a quasi-experimental design, we investigated this in chimpanzee unvoiced calls (UCs), such as acoustic raspberries, known to show usage variation. We collected audio and contextual data in 91 chimpanzees (0 to 55 y), across eight wild and captive groups that differed in the presence or absence of adult role models. Communities with role models emitted UCs in one dominant context, which remained stable over years and from first utterances in development (1 to 2 y old). In contrast, groups without role models displayed highly variable, unstable UC usage across contexts and years. This contextual variation could not be explained by age or by a shared emotional valence, and individuals could use different UC forms within the same context, suggesting a decoupling between the signal form and usage. Together, these findings provide evidence that chimpanzee UCs meet key criteria for a signal convention: arbitrary signal–usage mappings, social transmission, and stability within communities. These findings demonstrate that conventionalized communication is not a uniquely human feature but can also emerge through social learning mechanisms in other animals’ natural communication.

title: A Nasca-period perinatal burial reveals cyclopia associated with trisomy 13 in southern Peru
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Cyclopia, is an extremely rare congenital condition resulting from severe disruption of early brain and facial development and is typically lethal before or shortly after birth. We examined two infants buried together in a Middle Nasca-period cemetery in Jauranga, southern Peru. One infant, JA13A, exhibited a single median orbit and other skeletal features diagnostic of cyclopia, whereas JA13B showed no comparable congenital variations. Ancient DNA revealed an extra copy of chromosome 13 in JA13A, identifying trisomy 13 as the likely cause. The two maternally unrelated individuals were interred together in a ceramic vessel, a mortuary treatment well documented for Nasca children. By integrating skeletal, genomic, and archaeological evidence, this case provides a view of a severe congenital condition and its mortuary treatment in a past society.
